title: RBAC & Auth, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, and Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Consolidated guidance and operational workflows for RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC controls, incident-response security procedures, compliance evidence gathering, and risk & exceptions process.
body:
Purpose and scope

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's operational standards and repeatable workflows for security and compliance topics that cross multiple teams. It covers: RBAC and authentication, audit logging requirements and retention, data residency and retention tables, secure SDLC checkpoints, incident-response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows for audits, and the risk & exceptions process. Audience: security engineers, platform engineers, SREs, product managers, and compliance owners.

1) RBAC and authentication

Overview
- Objective: ensure least-privilege access to control plane and data plane services while enabling developer productivity.
- Scope: cloud control plane (GCP/AWS accounts), internal admin consoles, CI systems, Vault/KMS, private deployment control planes.

Roles and responsibilities
- Role taxonomy (high level):
  - org-admin: full administrative control over organization-level resources (very limited, requires 2FA + just-in-time elevation). Owner: Security.
  - platform-admin: manages platform infra (clusters, networking). Owner: Eng Infra.
  - service-owner: owns a specific service (runtime, routing, console). Owner: Eng Platform / Eng Serving Runtime.
  - dev: standard engineering access to dev/test resources only. Owner: Eng Teams.
  - support: scoped access for support tasks with timebound sessions and audit hooks. Owner: Customer Success.

Authentication standards
- All interactive access requires SSO with SAML/OIDC (Okta).
- Passwords are not allowed for critical consoles; enforce MFA (TOTP or hardware key).
- Machine identities: use short-lived service account tokens via workload identity where available (GKE Workload Identity, AWS STS).
- KMS/HSM key usage requires key policy binding and key-access approval workflow.

Authorization policies
- Implement RBAC via a single source of truth (IAM + central policy repo). All role definitions live in the security Git repository (security/iam/roles).
- Use attribute-based access controls (ABAC) for runtime-level controls (team, environment, project).
- Policy change process: 1) design PR, 2) security review, 3) canary rollout to staging, 4) full rollout and audit capture.

Just-in-time (JIT) elevation
- For sensitive operations (org-wide config changes, KMS key rotation, account billing), require JIT approval via the Access Request service. Approvals are recorded in the ticket and surfaced in audit logs.

2) Audit logging

Objectives
- Provide tamper-evident logs for authentication, authorization changes, administrative actions, and data access events. Support forensic investigations and compliance evidence requests.

What to log (minimum)
- Authentication events: successful & failed logins, MFA challenges, token issuance/refresh.
- Authorization changes: role assignments, policy changes, RBAC role creation/deletion.
- Administrative actions: deployments, config changes, secret rotations.
- Data access: read/write/delete on customer-controlled data stores, model artifacts, and sensitive config.
- System events: autoscale, instance termination, kernel panics, and image boot anomalies relevant to security.

Logging architecture and guarantees
- Centralized collection: all services forward structured logs (JSON) to Elasticsearch/Opensearch + cold archive in cloud object storage (S3/GCS).
- Integrity: enable write-once object store buckets with bucket policies; sign logs using a rotation-aware signing process.
- Retention and immutability: critical audit logs are retained in immutable storage for the configured retention period (see retention table).
- Monitoring: detect log-forwarder gaps with heartbeat monitors; alert if >5 min of missing telemetry.

Log format and fields (example)
- timestamp, principal (user/service), principal_id, action, resource_type, resource_id, src_ip, user_agent, outcome (success/failure), request_id, trace_id, extra (freeform).
- Example (single-line JSON): {"timestamp":"2026-06-01T15:12:08Z", "principal":"alice@example.com", "action":"iam.role.assign", "resource_type":"project", "resource_id":"proj-124", "outcome":"success"}

Alerting thresholds for audit telemetry
- Missing logs: alert if any service's log heartbeat missing for 5+ minutes.
- Elevated error rate: alert if auth failure rate increases by >200% over rolling 10m baseline.

3) Data residency and retention

Principles
- Customers may select region-bound data residency for private deployments and dedicated capacity. Redwood stores customer content and PII only in designated regions when requested.
- Retention should balance forensic needs, regulatory obligations, and customer SLA.
- Default retention values apply to hosted customers; enterprise contracts may specify alternate retention.

Retention policy matrix (table)
- NOTE: table represented as plain text for Confluence export.

| Data type | Default retention | Storage class | Responsible owner | Notes |
|-----------|------------------:|---------------|-------------------|-------|
| Auth & audit logs | 7 years | Cold/Immutable | Security | Required for SOC2/ISO evidence; immutable archive |
| Control-plane metrics (anonymized) | 3 years | Warm -> Cold | Eng SRE | Aggregated; no PII |
| PII associated with account (support tickets) | 7 years (or per contract) | Encrypted | Customer Success / Legal | Redaction available on request |
| Model artifacts & weights (customer-supplied) | Per contract | Customer-managed or encrypted archive | Customer | Default: customer controls retention in private deployments |
| Runtime ephemeral caches | 72 hours | Ephemeral | Eng Serving Runtime | KV caches flushed or encrypted on disk; can be disabled for private deployments |
| Backups (DB snapshots) | 90 days | Encrypted backup | Eng Infra | Snapshots encrypted with KMS keys per region |

Note: retention table must be reflected in terraform/state and backup manifests. See related_pages for implementation links.

Data residency controls
- Region binding: resources for a customer labelled with region tags and enforced via placement policies.
- Cross-region replication disabled by default for region-bound accounts; explicit change request + security review required.
- Data egress: any egress of customer data for support requires approval and must be tracked in the data access ledger.

4) Secure SDLC (controls and checkpoints)

Philosophy
- Security gates must be integrated into CI/CD to avoid manual bottlenecks but provide automated guardrails with human reviews for high-risk changes.

Required pipeline checks
- Pre-merge: static analysis (SAST), secret-scan, dependency vulnerability scan (Snyk/OSS scanner), and license checks.
- Post-merge: integration tests in isolated testnet with instrumentation for data access; dependency SBOM generation.
- Deploy pipeline: canary deploy + automatic RBAC and feature-flag validation; deploy requires passing security and perf gates.

High-risk change criteria (requires security review)
- Changes to IAM roles/policies, KMS/HSM config, log retention settings, or data residency flags.
- Modifying runtime encryption-at-rest or key rotation procedures.
- Adding third-party integrations that process PII or customer content.

Deployment checklist (example)
1) PR created with description of change, risk assessment, and rollback plan.
2) Automatic checks passed (SAST, secret-scan, unit tests).
3) Security reviewer approves if high-risk flag is set.
4) Canary deployment to staging with audit logging enabled.
5) Post-canary smoke tests and security telemetry reviewed.
6) Full rollout with post-deploy monitoring for 24 hours.

5) Incident response — security procedures

Objectives
- Ensure rapid detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and timely communication for security incidents affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of customer or platform assets.

Triage and severity classification
- Sev1 (Critical): active data exfiltration, production control-plane outage >30 min impacting >10% customers, or confirmed compromise of KMS/HSM keys.
- Sev2 (High): limited data exposure, degraded control-plane impacting <10% customers, suspected lateral movement.
- Sev3 (Medium): service degradation with no clear security impact, or security findings requiring patch.

Initial response steps (playbook)
1) Detection: Incident detected via telemetry, SSO alerts, or external report.
2) Declare incident in PagerDuty with severity classification.
3) Assemble incident response (IR) pod: Incident Commander (IC), SRE lead, Security lead, PR/Comms, Legal.
4) Triage: preserve logs, snapshot affected systems, collect volatile evidence (in-memory if applicable).
5) Contain: apply ACLs, rotate compromised credentials, isolate nodes, and revoke suspicious sessions.
6) Communicate: post initial status to status.redwood.com and internal #incidents channel within 1 hour of declaration (template below).
7) Investigate & eradicate: root cause analysis, remove persistence mechanisms.
8) Recovery: restore from known-good backups, validate integrity, and bring systems back under monitoring.
9) Post-incident: produce postmortem and compliance packet within 14 calendar days.

Evidence preservation checklist
- Capture timeline of events, relevant audit logs, affected resource IDs, signed snapshots of logs, memory dumps where required, and chain-of-custody notes.
- Ensure evidence stored in the secure evidence bucket with write-once flags.

Communication template (initial post)
- Title: [INCIDENT] <short description> — Severity Sx
- Summary: When detected, brief impact statement (customers affected, functionality).
- Actions taken: containment steps executed.
- Next steps: investigation owner, expected update cadence (every 2 hours for Sev1).
- Contact: incident commander and security lead.

6) Compliance evidence workflows (SOC2/ISO/GDPR readiness)

Who owns evidence?
- Security owns audit logs, controls mapping, and evidence packaging. Owners of services must provide attestations and artifact links (runbooks, config diffs, screenshots of consoles where needed).

Standard evidence package (for a control)
- Control description and mapping to framework (e.g., SOC2 CC6).
- Relevant artifacts: policy document, IAM policy file, example audit logs (redacted if PII), screenshots of settings, configuration management state (git commit IDs), and deployment-time signatures.
- Evidence hash: computed SHA256 of the zipped evidence bundle stored in evidence-bucket.

Evidence request process
1) Request via Compliance ticketing queue (Jira project: INFRA-COMP).
2) Security triages and assigns to service owner.
3) Service owner collects artifacts and uploads to evidence bucket following naming convention: evidence/<control-id>/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<service>.zip.
4) Security validates artifact completeness within 5 business days and marks request resolved.

Automated evidence collectors
- Where possible, use automated collectors (scripts run by CI) to produce SBOMs, deployment receipts, and audit snapshots. Manual artifacts must include an attestation signed by the service owner.

7) Risk and exceptions process

Purpose
- Document situations where strict enforcement of a control would cause unacceptable operational risk. Exceptions are temporary, timeboxed, and require compensating controls.

Exception request workflow
1) Open an Exception Request in the Exceptions tracker (link) with: control impacted, justification, duration (max 90 days), risk assessment, and mitigation plan.
2) Security reviews and classifies risk level (Low/Medium/High).
3) For High-risk exceptions, present to Risk Committee for approval.
4) Approved exceptions are time-bound and must include monitoring requirements and a remediation owner.

Required fields for exception requests
- control_id, business_rationale, estimated_impact, compensating_controls, remediation_plan, remediation_date, requestor, approver.

Renewal and closure
- Exceptions automatically expire; renewal requires demonstration of progress. On remediation, service owner must provide evidence of closure and update the config repo to eliminate the exception.

8) Operational runbooks & ownership

Key owners
- Security: policy, audit integrity, incident response coordination, evidence packaging.
- Eng SRE: monitoring, runbook execution, and checkpointing retention exports.
- Eng Infra: backups, KMS, region placement enforcement.
- Service Owners: attestations, per-service logs, and remediation.

Runbooks to maintain (minimum)
- RBAC change rollouts and rollback runbook.
- Audit-log gap detection & recovery runbook.
- Data-residency violation response runbook.
- Incident evidence capture runbook.

9) Appendix: quick commands and templates

Evidence upload naming convention (example)
- evidence/CC6/2026-06-01_runtime-service.zip

Sample jq filter for extracting suspicious auth failures
- jq 'select(.action=="auth.login" and .outcome=="failure") | {timestamp, principal, src_ip, user_agent, request_id}'

Initial incident post template (copy/paste)
- Title: [INCIDENT] Unauthorized access detected — Severity S1
- Summary: Detected at <time>. Limited number of unauthenticated sessions observed on the console; potential data access.
- Actions taken: Rotated affected API keys, isolated affected nodes, preserved logs.
- Next update: in 2 hours. IC: @<name> Security Lead: @<name>
